definition: How well findings transfer beyond the tested population, setting, or conditions.
example: Check whether a benchmark gain holds in deployment.
caveat: A large test set can still have poor external validity.

definition: A tree ensemble that increases randomness in split thresholds and feature selection.
example: Fit a fast randomized tabular baseline.
caveat: More randomness can increase bias while reducing variance.

definition: Predicting outside the range or support represented by observed data.
example: Forecast behavior at values beyond the training range.
caveat: Performance can degrade sharply outside familiar data.

definition: A weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall with beta controlling recall emphasis.
example: Weight missed positives more heavily.
caveat: It is not a universal cost-sensitive utility function.

definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall.
example: Summarize positive-class retrieval performance.
caveat: It ignores true negatives and embeds a particular tradeoff.

definition: A latent-variable model explaining correlations using shared factors and observation-specific noise.
example: Model correlated measurements with hidden factors.
caveat: Its noise model distinguishes it from basic PCA.

definition: A family of normative and statistical goals concerning equitable model treatment or outcomes.
example: Evaluate performance and error differences across relevant groups.
caveat: No single metric captures all fairness concerns.

definition: Agreement between an explanation, rationale, or generated answer and the mechanism or source evidence it claims to reflect.
example: Check whether a cited passage actually supports an answer.
caveat: Mechanistic faithfulness and source faithfulness are different uses.

definition: Simulating quantization and dequantization effects in a differentiable training workflow.
example: Expose a model to low-precision rounding during QAT.
caveat: The stored tensor may remain floating point.

definition: The expected proportion of false rejections among rejected hypotheses under a specified procedure.
example: Control false discoveries across many experiments.
caveat: Different from controlling the chance of any false positive.

definition: A positive case incorrectly predicted as negative.
example: Miss a target event.
caveat: Reducing false negatives can increase false positives.

definition: The fraction of actual positive cases predicted negative.
example: Measure missed detections among positives.
caveat: It equals one minus recall in the same binary setup.

definition: A case incorrectly predicted as belonging to the positive class.
example: Flag a legitimate event as anomalous.
caveat: Costs depend on the application.

definition: The fraction of actual negative cases predicted positive.
example: Measure false alarms among negative examples.
caveat: Its denominator differs from false discovery proportion.

definition: An input variable or representation used by a model.
example: House area is a feature for price prediction.
caveat: Features may be learned rather than hand-designed.

definition: Assigning input or internal features contribution scores for a particular output.
example: Estimate which words affect a prediction.
caveat: Attribution methods make different assumptions and can disagree.

definition: Training a student to match selected teacher intermediate representations.
example: Align hidden features between networks.
caveat: Different hidden dimensions may require projection layers.

definition: Designing input variables or transformations using task knowledge.
example: Create time-since-last-purchase from event timestamps.
caveat: Engineered features can leak target information.

definition: Converting raw inputs into a useful representation.
example: Extract image descriptors or text embeddings.
caveat: Extraction can be learned or manually defined.

definition: An array of activations describing where a learned feature occurs in an input.
example: Track locations that activate a texture detector.
caveat: Feature maps need not correspond to human-interpretable concepts.

definition: Changing feature magnitudes to improve numerical behavior or comparability.
example: Scale distance-based model inputs.
caveat: Tree models and distance-based models respond differently.

definition: Choosing a subset of available input features.
example: Remove redundant predictors before fitting a model.
caveat: Perform selection inside cross-validation to avoid leakage.

definition: A learned feature dividing into more specific features as representation or dictionary capacity increases.
example: Compare sparse autoencoders of different widths.
caveat: Splitting patterns are empirical, not guaranteed semantic hierarchies.

definition: A system for managing, discovering, and serving reusable features with consistent definitions.
example: Share validated features across models and environments.
caveat: A feature store does not automatically eliminate leakage.

definition: An ordered collection of feature values representing one item.
example: Encode a home as area, age, and rooms.
caveat: Feature order and preprocessing must stay consistent.

definition: Training across separate data holders while coordinating model updates instead of centralizing raw data.
example: Train across devices with local datasets.
caveat: Federation alone does not guarantee privacy.

definition: A network where information flows without recurrent feedback through the computation graph.
example: Transform each token independently within a Transformer block.
caveat: A feed-forward component can be part of a larger recurrent system.

definition: Adapting or performing a task using only a small number of examples.
example: Classify a new category from five examples.
caveat: Few-shot prompting may not change model weights.

definition: Providing a small number of task examples within the context.
example: Show three input-output examples before a new query.
caveat: The examples do not ordinarily update model weights.

definition: Training or prompting a model to generate missing content between a prefix and suffix.
example: Complete code within an existing function.
caveat: The model must understand the relevant formatting convention.

definition: Continuing training from an existing checkpoint for a task, domain, or behavior.
example: Adapt a pretrained model to support conversations.
caveat: It can change unrelated capabilities and safety behavior.

definition: A matrix measuring local sensitivity of a likelihood to parameter changes in expectation.
example: Define a probabilistic model's local geometry.
caveat: Empirical and expected Fisher matrices are not always interchangeable.

definition: An IO-aware implementation of exact attention reducing memory traffic through tiling and recomputation.
example: Train attention models with lower memory overhead.
caveat: It optimizes execution rather than changing the attention objective.

definition: A 16-bit floating-point format with lower storage cost but a narrower numeric range than float32.
example: Reduce activation memory and accelerate supported operations.
caveat: Its limited range can cause overflow or underflow.

definition: A 32-bit floating-point representation commonly used for numerical computation and model state.
example: Keep sensitive accumulations in single precision.
caveat: Floating-point arithmetic is approximate even at this precision.

definition: A family of eight-bit floating-point formats used in supported low-precision computation.
example: Reduce memory traffic in suitable model operations.
caveat: FP8 is not one universal format or a guaranteed accuracy-preserving switch.

definition: A count of floating-point arithmetic operations used to describe computational work.
example: Estimate training computation.
caveat: A work count is not a speed measurement.

definition: A rate of floating-point arithmetic computation.
example: Compare theoretical compute rates at a specified precision.
caveat: Peak FLOPS does not directly predict end-to-end model speed.

definition: Training a vector field to match a chosen probability path between distributions, enabling generation through continuous transport.
example: Learn a generative flow from noise to data.
caveat: Flow matching is a training framework, not synonymous with all normalizing flows.

definition: A classification loss downweighting easy examples relative to hard ones.
example: Train a detector with many easy background examples.
caveat: It changes calibration and introduces additional hyperparameters.

definition: Predicting future values from historical and contextual information.
example: Forecast hourly electricity demand.
caveat: Random splits can leak future information.

definition: Automatic differentiation propagating directional derivatives alongside values.
example: Compute a Jacobian-vector product.
caveat: It is often advantageous when input directions are few.

definition: A broadly pretrained model that can be adapted or prompted for multiple downstream tasks.
example: Adapt a pretrained text model to classification.
caveat: Foundation models are not limited to language.

definition: A decoding penalty depending on how often a token has already appeared.
example: Discourage repeatedly used words.
caveat: Formula and token accounting depend on the serving implementation.

definition: The square root of the sum of squared matrix entries.
example: Measure a weight matrix's total magnitude.
caveat: Not generally the same as the spectral norm.

definition: Attention allowing all positions permitted by the general mask to interact.
example: Use all earlier tokens in causal self-attention.
caveat: A causal mask still permits dense attention over the prefix.

definition: Updating all or nearly all model parameters during adaptation.
example: Specialize an entire model on domain data.
caveat: It usually needs more trainable-state memory than adapter methods.

definition: A distributed training approach that shards model state across data-parallel workers and gathers needed pieces for computation.
example: Train larger models with less memory per GPU.
caveat: Sharding saves persistent memory but adds communication.

definition: Producing structured requests to invoke named functions with arguments.
example: Return a search function name and query argument.
caveat: A well-formed call can still be unauthorized or semantically wrong.

definition: A block multiplying one learned projection by a gate derived from another.
example: Control feature flow in a feed-forward block.
caveat: The gate's activation differs across GLU variants.
